newsitem.title: INDIA: India touts investment in ports, roads.
newsitem.headline: India touts investment in ports, roads.

text.p: Better rules and an anticipated cooling of interest rates make the time ripe for foreigners to invest in much-needed ports and roads, a government minister said on Tuesday.

Yogendra Alagh, junior planning minister, told a seminar on ports and roads in the Indian capital that the establishment of a tariff authority to fix and revise port charges meant such charges would always be sufficient to recoup the costs of operators.
"Indian tariff authorities have been generally concerned about long-term costing," he said. Later, Alagh told Reuters: "What this means is that capital costs will be taken care of (by tariffs)."
"The system now is very transparent. The rules are known," Alagh said during the seminar.
Ports and roads are receiving close attention from the Indian government, which launched a programme of economic liberalisation in 1991.
Authorities are keen to build quality infrastructure to keep the economy growing at seven percent or more a year.
Last year, the government announced guidelines for private investors to build ports along India's 6,000 kilometres (3,750 miles) coastline.
Moreover, major Indian ports were considering proposals for private investment worth 63.5 billion rupees ($1.7 billion), Alagh said.

The government also has identified potential highway projects for which build-operate-transfer (BOT) contracts will be awarded to private firms, which can levy toll charges. Road builders also will enjoy five-year tax holidays.

The Indian budget for 1997/98 (April-March) has allocated five billion rupees ($139 million) to fund the capital base of the National Highway Authority of India, which oversees privatisation of highways.

Investment needs have been estimated at 800 billion rupees ($22.3 billion) for roads and 254 billion ($7 billion) for ports by 2005/06. Port cargo is expected to grow to 650 million tonnes by 2005/06 from 240 million tonnes in 1996/97.

Alagh said New Delhi's macroeconomic policies were being adjusted to ensure that Indian interest rates gradually come down to world norms. "Don't at first glance be disturbed that interest rates are higher in India," he said.
Officials say ports need electronic equipment, container facilities and coordination with other means of transport to improve efficiency.
Alagh said foreign investors had to bear the exchange rate risks associated with their investments, but a senior official said later that the government was trying to minimise it.
"I am sure this question will be addressed very favourably by the authority (for tariffs)," Pankaj Jain, development adviser in charge of ports in the Surface Transport Ministry, told the seminar.

Besides the establishment of the tariff authority, the government was also in the process of setting up a national regulator for ports, Jain said. India was also willing to make further policy changes to help investors, he added.
The government had finalised 28 proposals involving private investments in ports since 1991, Jain said.
Officials are also keen to boost a market for long-term debt, which they believe holds the key to funding a voracious hunger for infrastructure. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
